strengths: UniAP addresses a useful training-systems problem: coordinating pipeline placement with DP, TP, and FSDP choices under communication and memory constraints. Its application to large vision Transformers gives it clear relevance to computer vision.

Table 1 reports meaningful measured gains. On ENVB-8, ViT throughput increases from 38.74 samples/s for Alpa and 32.20 for Galvatron to 45.58; Swin improves from 13.90 to 19.08 over Galvatron. The reported 3.80× Llama speedup further demonstrates potential usefulness.

Evaluation covers four hardware environments, multiple Transformer architectures, and weak scaling to 64 DCUs. Matching the best enumerated Megatron strategy while substantially reducing search time is also practically valuable.

The workflow, pseudocode, hardware specifications, model configurations, and solver settings provide useful implementation detail. Appendix F reports 3.59% average throughput-estimation error on selected strategies, providing some support for the cost model.
weaknesses: The stated formulation has a consequential ordering gap. Equation (6) enforces contiguity but does not enforce pipeline-stage order. For a two-layer chain u→v, placing u on stage 2 and v on stage 1 satisfies the contiguity and placement constraints, yet Equation (4) counts zero communication for this edge. The optimizer can therefore favor an incorrectly costed placement. Appendix B proves contiguity only and does not resolve this problem.

The connection to the claimed MIQP implementation is incomplete. Expanding Equations (3)–(4) produces products of four binary variables involving two placement and two strategy indicators. Auxiliary variables and a reformulation are needed to obtain the stated quadratic formulation, but these are not supplied. This is potentially correctable, yet it prevents reproducing the central optimization model as written.

The GPipe memory constraint is insufficiently explained. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c into CostModeling, and Section 3.2 scales activation memory with that input. GPipe retains activations from multiple forward micro-batches before backward execution, but the formulation does not explain how this accumulation enters Equation (5). Consequently, its claim to ensure memory feasibility is not adequately supported; no memory-estimation validation is reported.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the demonstrated guarantees. Appendix E specifies a 60-second limit and early termination with a relative optimality gap below 4%, while achieved gaps and timeout outcomes are not reported. Section 3.5 obtains its runtime bound by treating solver time as constant; this does not establish the complexity of finding an optimum. Moreover, accuracy on selected strategies does not establish correct ranking throughout the candidate space.

The experiments do not isolate the central claim that joint optimization improves on hierarchical optimization. Figure 6 compares against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only restrictions, rather than a hierarchical variant using the same cost model, execution backend, and candidate strategies. Appendix F also reports different cost-model accuracies between UniAP and Galvatron, providing another possible explanation for gains. Hierarchical decomposition alone does not imply suboptimality.

Search-time comparisons require qualification: UniAP measures UOP time without profiling, and Section 4.2 attributes substantial gains to multithreaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baselines. These are useful operational results, but they do not establish equivalent-budget algorithmic superiority or total setup savings. The measured benefits merit consideration, but the formulation errors and incomplete validation of the central optimization claim currently determine my weak-reject recommendation.
